rows.selection_reason: With no completed experiments, the most important uncertainty is whether a standard multimodal pipeline (combining RNA and image features) provides a viable and competitive baseline. config_001 uses the most established RNA encoder (scgpt), the strongest pre-trained image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), the simplest profile setting (singleprofile, removing aggregation as a confound), and a simple weighted fusion. This makes it a clean, 'default' multimodal reference point. It is the best first experiment because: (1) it tests the core hypothesis of the study—that multimodal fusion is beneficial—using well-validated components so that any result is not confounded by an unusual encoder choice; (2) it establishes a performance anchor against which all subsequent multimodal variants (multiprofile, different fusion, different encoders) and single-modality baselines (image-only config_017, RNA-only config_011) can be directly compared; and (3) by keeping the design simple (singleprofile, weighted fusion), it isolates the fundamental question of whether the two modalities are complementary before adding complexity. This maximizes the information gained per experiment under the limited budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion → 0.4224 acc), the most critical uncertainty is whether the multimodal fusion actually adds value over a unimodal baseline. config_017 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) is the cleanest single-axis comparison: it uses the same image encoder and profile setting as config_001, removing only the RNA modality and fusion step. If image-only achieves comparable accuracy, the RNA contribution (and all downstream RNA-encoder/fusion questions) is deprioritized; if it is substantially lower, multimodal fusion is confirmed as a productive direction and subsequent experiments can focus on optimizing RNA encoder, aggregation, and fusion. This experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the single most important architectural decision before spending further budget on finer-grained multimodal variants.

With only two completed experiments, the most critical uncertainty is the individual contribution of each modality. We know image-only (config_017, ViT-L) yields acc=0.227, and multimodal (config_001, scgpt+ViT-L, weighted fusion) yields acc=0.422. Testing RNA-only with the same scgpt encoder and singleprofile setting (config_011) directly decomposes the multimodal gain: if RNA-only approaches 0.40, the image adds little and we should focus on RNA encoder/fusion choices; if it is near 0.20–0.25, the image contributes substantially and image encoder improvements become high-value. This single experiment reduces the largest source of uncertainty in the design space and will guide whether subsequent budget is better spent on image-side or RNA-side improvements. It is a clean, single-variable comparison to config_001 (only the modality is removed), making interpretation straightforward under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_001 (multimodal, scgpt+imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion) achieves 0.4224 acc, only marginally above RNA-only config_011 (0.4106 acc), while image-only config_017 is far weaker (0.2266). This suggests the image modality contributes very little, possibly because the weighted fusion strategy is not effectively leveraging it. Question: Does changing fusion from weighted to concat (the only difference in config_006) meaningfully alter the multimodal gain over RNA-only? Why this experiment: It is a clean single-variable comparison against our best result, isolating the fusion mechanism. If concat yields a substantially different result, we learn that fusion strategy is a key lever and should be prioritized in all future multimodal runs. If it is similar, we can rule out fusion as the bottleneck and redirect effort toward RNA encoder choice, image encoder, or multiprofile aggregation. Under a limited budget, resolving this binary question with one experiment is the most efficient use of the next slot.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: All four completed experiments use singleprofile with no aggregation. We know RNA (scgpt) dominates (0.4106 rna_only vs 0.2266 image_only), that multimodal concat fusion (config_006, 0.4348) modestly beats weighted (config_001, 0.4224), and that the image modality adds only ~2% over RNA alone. However, the profile-setting axis (single vs. multi) is completely unexplored, representing the largest remaining source of architectural uncertainty. 2) What this tests: config_005 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) is the minimal-change extension of our best result (config_006) to the multiprofile regime—only the profile setting and the required aggregation (avgpool) change, while keeping the same RNA encoder, image encoder, and concat fusion. This cleanly isolates whether multiple profiles with average-pool aggregation improve over a single profile. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: The profile/aggregation axis is the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact design question remaining. Testing it with the simplest aggregation (avgpool) and holding all other variables at their best-known values (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, concat) follows the principle of changing as few factors as possible. A positive result would open the multiprofile design space for further exploitation; a null or negative result would justify concentrating the remaining budget on singleprofile refinements (e.g., RNA encoder choice, image encoder choice). Either outcome substantially reduces uncertainty about a core architectural decision under a tight budget.

The strongest result so far is config_005 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) at 0.5176 accuracy, a large jump over the best singleprofile result (config_006 at 0.4348). This shows that multiprofile with aggregation is highly beneficial. The most important open question is whether the aggregation method matters: avgpool is a simple mean, while a transformer can model inter-profile interactions. config_020 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, transformer, concat) differs from config_005 only in aggregation (transformer vs avgpool), giving a clean, single-variable comparison. If transformer outperforms avgpool, it identifies a new promising direction for further exploration; if avgpool is sufficient or better, it confirms a simpler, more efficient design and redirects effort toward other factors (RNA encoder, image encoder, fusion). This is the highest-information next step because it directly extends the best-performing configuration while isolating one critical design choice under a limited budget.

Evidence: The dominant finding is that multiprofile provides a large gain (~8 pts) over singleprofile (config_005: 0.518 vs config_006: 0.435), and within multiprofile, avgpool+concat with scgpt+imagenet_vit_l is the current best. However, the RNA encoder axis is completely unexplored—we have only tested scgpt. Since RNA is the dominant signal (rna_only 0.411 vs image_only 0.227), the quality of the RNA representation is likely the next most impactful design lever. Question: Does switching the RNA encoder from scgpt to scvi_n200 (another learned, generative-style representation) improve or degrade performance in the multiprofile setting? config_034 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat, multiprofile) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_005, isolating the RNA encoder effect while holding all other design choices constant. Why best next experiment: It tests the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact unexplored axis (RNA representation) in the regime where performance is already highest, with a minimal change that cleanly attributes any performance shift to the encoder choice. The result will determine whether to invest further in learned RNA encoders or pivot to linear (PCA) representations, and will guide all subsequent experiments on the image encoder and fusion axes.

The strongest result so far is config_034 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 acc, driven primarily by the scvi_n200 RNA encoder. The key open question is whether the aggregation method over multiple profiles can further improve performance with this much richer representation. With the weaker scgpt encoder, avgpool marginally beat transformer (0.518 vs 0.507), but that gap was small and may not hold with scvi_n200's higher-dimensional, more structured embeddings where inter-profile interactions might be better captured by a transformer. config_008 changes only the aggregation (avgpool → transformer) while holding all other settings identical to config_034, giving a clean single-variable comparison. This is the best use of the next experiment because it directly exploits the strongest evidence while isolating the effect of aggregation, which is a critical architectural choice for multiprofile models and could unlock further gains or confirm that simple averaging is sufficient.

The two best experiments (config_034: 0.715, config_008: 0.721) both use scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile, showing that the RNA encoder choice is the dominant factor. However, we have no RNA-only baseline with scvi_n200 + multiprofile, so we cannot determine whether the image modality is actually contributing meaningful complementary information or whether the high performance is driven entirely by the RNA encoder. With scgpt, the image added only ~0.02 over RNA-alone (0.411 vs 0.435), suggesting the image contribution may be marginal. Config_025 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) is a clean single-variable ablation of config_034 (removing the image). If RNA alone approaches ~0.70, the image is not adding value and we can simplify the pipeline; if it drops to ~0.50–0.60, the image is providing substantial complementary signal and further image-encoder or fusion experiments become high-priority. Under a limited budget, resolving this fundamental modality-contribution question is more informative than a small fusion-method tweak (e.g., weighted vs concat) that is unlikely to change the ranking of top configurations.

Evidence: The top two configs (config_008: 0.7207, config_034: 0.7150) both use scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile + concat fusion, differing only in aggregation (transformer vs avgpool, a negligible ~0.006 gap). However, we have not yet tested weighted fusion in this high-performing regime—our only fusion comparisons so far were in the weaker scgpt regime (config_001 vs config_006, ~0.01 gap). Question: Does weighted fusion outperform or match concat when the RNA encoder is scvi_n200 and the image encoder is imagenet_vit_l with transformer aggregation? This is a clean single-variable comparison to our current best (config_008), isolating the fusion effect. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly exploits the strongest evidence (scvi_n200 + multiprofile + imagenet_vit_l) while resolving an important, still-uncertain design choice (fusion strategy) in the regime that actually matters. A result here either improves on the current best or confirms concat as the preferred fusion, freeing subsequent budget to test image-encoder alternatives.
